paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Majuli, in the northeast Indian state of Assam, is the largest river island in the world, with a population of around 170,000 people belonging to 11 ethnic groups. But over the past 50 years, soil erosion and flooding have robbed the picturesque island of much of its area and vegetation, destroying the livelihoods of the people who live there.

The monsoon season is particularly difficult. 'We are completely cut off from the rest of the world for nearly four to five months every year when the floodwater submerges our homes and fields, leaving us marooned on the island,' says Rombha Payeng. 'Luckily, the bao paddy [flood-resistant red rice] that grows here helps us to run our livelihood.' But she explains that until recently, the vegetables planted to supplement the rice were washed away in the floodwater, and her two daughters were not getting a healthy diet.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: According to Irshad Ali, the sub-divisional agricultural officer for Majuli, around 9,270 hectares of land is cultivated on the island, with 31,420 people dependent on this for their livelihood. In response to the destruction of crops by flooding, the South Asian Forum for Environment (SAFE), a non-profit organisation working to advance sustainable development, has introduced a new method to help people cope with the increasingly unstable climate — floating agriculture.

Chiranjeet Chatterjee, the director of programmes at SAFE, says that they initially adopted a hydroponics method of farming, where plants are grown in nutrient-rich water instead of soil, on floating rafts. Vegetables were grown in water-soaked, non-biodegradable sponge material on bamboo rafts. Farmers were able to grow some vegetables but it was not a long-term solution, Chatterjee explains, because the rafts tended to rot.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Now a new method has been introduced which involves supporting the rafts on drums, meaning they are not directly in contact with the water. Instead of growing vegetables in sponge beds, they are now cultivated in grow bags on the rafts. These are filled with compost, a type of charcoal called biochar, sawdust and organic fertilisers.

As well as being watered manually by the farmers, the plants are watered by solar-powered pumps. These pump water up into the grow bags, through an irrigation system installed on the raft. The grow bags retain moisture and minimise water loss, while excess water can drain away into the pond through holes in the bags. The entire structure is covered with netting to stop birds from eating the harvest. Because the rafts rise with the water level, flooding does not damage crops grown on them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Saben Kalita, a field coordinator at SAFE, says that each raft can accommodate 25 grow bags. Currently, there are 55 of the new type of raft being used by farmers on Majuli, Kalita says. 'The method is cost-effective in comparison with traditional agriculture with no requirement of tilling and sowing.'

Pointing to rafts laden with beds of crops floating on the water near her stilt house, Rombha says, 'The situation has changed now, as my daughters ate ladyfingers [okra] and other vegetables for the first time this year.' Bolin Payeng, Rombha's husband, says he is pleased with the new floating farm beds. 'The floating beds have long-term durability and help us to grow vegetables of our choice and feed them to our families, besides selling them in the market.'

Arun Kumar Pathak, a retired district agriculture officer in Majuli, says, 'Floating farm beds have helped [farmers] to cultivate vegetables, shrubs and medicinal plants. The method encourages organic farming.' Other benefits of floating farms are that they require less space than conventional farming and do not need pesticides.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: 'We have cultivated around 25–30 kilogrammes of king chilli … along with 45–50 kilogrammes of ladyfingers and bottle gourd from 20 trays this year,' says Jonaram Payeng, another farmer in Majuli (not a relative of Rombha Payeng). 'The vegetables are fresh and completely organic. We consumed most of them and sold the rest.'

Jonaram also grows flood-resistant paddy on his 0.40 hectares of land. He says that as the monsoon becomes more unpredictable, more farmers might need to turn to methods like floating farm beds. 'We depend on bao paddy for our livelihood and the floods are an important phenomenon as the paddy grows under the water, but there have been no major floods this year.' Ordinarily, flooding prevents farmers from growing vegetables. But this year the opposite has happened: a lack of rain has damaged the paddy crop.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Until now the farmers using floating rafts on Majuli have only made small profits by selling their crops to local markets. The main use of the crops has been to help provide better nutrition to families. But Chatterjee says that as the project expands, there is hope for greater profits – especially as all the materials required, including the compost, are available to farmers on the island.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Government officials from the state agriculture department say that floating farms are the future of agriculture on Majuli. 'The technique is not only helpful for this island but also for low-lying areas in other parts of the country that suffer crop loss and other damages due to floods,' Ali says. He added that his department has started another project on Majuli using water hyacinth to create floating organic vegetable beds. 'Such efforts need sustained long-term support from the government.'

To solve this problem, {{24}} are now placed under the rafts, keeping them away from the water. The vegetables are grown in bags filled with compost and other substances.
